pages.title: Obsidian Bases (.base files)
pages.description: Open, embed and edit Obsidian Bases files — what is supported, what is not, and how the golden set is checked.
pages.md:
A vault that comes from Obsidian keeps its **Bases**: `.base` files (YAML)
that turn notes into tables, cards, lists, kanban boards and maps. Lumen
reads and writes the same files, so the views survive the move both ways.

## Three ways to show a base

- **Open the `.base` file** from the workspace: the preview shows its views
  (one tab per view). The editor still shows the YAML.
- **Embed it in a note**: `![[Books.base]]` alone on a line, or
  `![[Books.base#Favourites]]` for one view.
- **Write it inline** in a fenced block:

````markdown
```base
filters:
  and:
    - file.hasTag("book")
    - 'status != "read"'
formulas:
  hours: (pages / 50).round(1)
views:
  - type: table
    name: To read
    order: [file.name, note.author, formula.hours]
    sort:
      - property: formula.hours
        direction: ASC
```
````

## What is supported

| Part of the file | Supported |
|---|---|
| `filters:` — a statement, or nested `and:` / `or:` / `not:` lists | yes (`not:` matches when none of its items match) |
| `formulas:` — computed properties, `formula.<name>`, a formula may use another | yes (a formula that refers to itself is reported) |
| `properties:` — `displayName` for column headers | yes |
| `summaries:` — your own summary formulas over `values` | yes |
| `views:` — `type`, `name`, `filters`, `order`, `sort`, `groupBy`, `limit`, `summaries` | yes |
| View types `table`, `cards` (`image:`), `list`, `kanban` (by `groupBy`), `map` (`coordinates:`) | yes |
| Plugin view types | shown as a table |
| Built-in summaries Average, Min, Max, Sum, Range, Median, Stddev, Earliest, Latest, Checked, Unchecked, Empty, Filled, Unique | yes |
| `this` — the `.base` file when opened, the embedding note when embedded | yes |

Expressions use the Bases language: `note.x` (or just `x`), `file.x`,
`formula.x`, `this.file.x`; operators `+ - * / %`, `== != < <= > >=`,
`! && ||`; text, numbers, lists `[a, b]`, regular expressions `/a.c/i`;
date arithmetic with durations (`today() - "1w"`, `date(note.due) + "1M"`).

**Functions:** 66 of the 68 functions in the Bases reference run (97 %):
all global functions except `icon()`, and every method on any value, text,
numbers, dates, lists (including `map`, `filter`, `reduce` with `value`,
`index`, `acc`), links, files, objects and regular expressions.

Not supported, with a clear message instead of a wrong value:

- `icon()` — the error reads "Bases function icon() is not supported here yet".
  Obsidian's icon set is too large to load in a note.
- `html()` — shown as plain text, never as markup (counted as not supported).

## Differences to know

- **Dates are UTC.** `today()` is the UTC date, as in database formulas, so a
  base gives the same answer on every machine.
- **`file.name` includes the extension** (`Dune.md`), as in Obsidian;
  `file.basename` is `Dune`.
- **`file.ctime`** is the modification time: the browser's file storage does
  not keep a creation time.
- **Text order** is natural (`2` before `10`), Latin before Hebrew.

## Sorting and saving

Click a column header to sort (again to reverse). For an embedded base,
**Save this sort to …** writes the new `sort:` into that view of the `.base`
file — comments, key order and everything else in the file stay as they
were. Opening and saving a base without edits keeps the same YAML data.

## Golden set

`src/__tests__/fixtures/bases/` holds 20 `.base` files and the vault they
run over (`vault.ts`). `expected.json` lists, for each file, the rows and
their order, and some values, worked out by hand from the Bases rules. The
test `basesGolden.test.ts` checks all 20, and that each file read and
written back unedited holds the same YAML.

To confirm against Obsidian 1.14: create the notes of `vault.ts` in an empty
vault, copy the 20 `.base` files into it, open each one and compare its
first view with `expected.json`. Any difference is a bug to file.

## Relations and rollups (Lumen)

Two top-level keys add Notion-style relations and rollups. They are a Lumen
extension: the file stays valid YAML, but Obsidian does not read these keys,
so their columns are empty there.

```yaml
relations:
  tasks:                 # notes whose `project` property links here
    property: project
    incoming: true
  team: members          # the notes this note's `members` links point to
rollups:
  hours:    { relation: tasks, property: estimate, function: sum }
  open:     { relation: tasks, function: count }
  next_due: { relation: tasks, property: due, function: earliest }
  cost:     { relation: team, property: rate, function: sum }
views:
  - type: table
    name: Projects
    order: [file.name, relation.tasks, rollup.hours, rollup.next_due]
```

- A **relation** follows a link property: one `[[link]]` or a list of
  them, as Obsidian writes them (aliases and paths resolve like any link).
  Outgoing by default: the notes the property points to. With
  `incoming: true` it runs the other way: the notes whose property points
  at this one. That gives you both sides of a link without writing it twice.
- A **rollup** computes `count`, `sum`, `avg`, `min`, `max`, `earliest` or
  `latest` over a property of the related notes. That can be `note.x`,
  `file.x`, one of the base's formulas (`formula.x`, computed for each
  related note), or another rollup.
- In a view, the columns are `relation.<name>` and `rollup.<name>`.
  Their headers are the names, unless `properties:` gives them a
  `displayName`.

## Calendar and timeline views (Lumen)

```yaml
views:
  - type: calendar
    name: Due
    date: due            # default: date
  - type: timeline
    name: Phases
    date: start
    end: finish          # optional: without it an item is one day long
```

- **Calendar** shows a month with each note on the day of its date.
  **Timeline** shows a bar from the start date to the end date for each note.
- To move a note to another day, drag it, or focus it and press
  **Alt + ←/→** for a day, **Alt + ↑/↓** for a week (the arrows follow the
  text direction, so in Hebrew → moves back). Only that date property changes in the note's file; every other byte
  stays as it was. A timeline bar keeps its length, so its end moves by
  the same number of days.
- In Obsidian these view types show as a table.

## Big bases and CSV

- A table of more than 200 rows draws only the rows in sight, so 10,000
  rows scroll smoothly. Filtering and sorting 10,000 notes takes well under
  100 ms.
- **Export CSV** saves the current view: its columns and rows, UTF-8 with a
  BOM, so Excel opens Hebrew correctly.
- **Import CSV…** adds one note per row to a folder named after the base:
  - The first column is the note's name.
  - The other columns become properties: numbers, `true` / `false` and
    text, with Hebrew headers kept.
  - Properties the base's filter pins (such as `type == "task"`) are added,
    so the new notes show in the view.
  - A name that's taken gets a number.

## Real vaults

The golden set was written from the Bases documentation. To check Lumen
against files people really write, `src/__tests__/fixtures/obsidian-corpus/`
holds byte-for-byte copies of seven public vaults with open licences (MIT,
and MIT + CC BY 4.0), each pinned to a commit in `manifest.json` with its
licence and a SHA-256 per file: 333 notes, 44 `.base` files and a canvas,
with callouts, `%%` comments, embeds, block ids, frontmatter and Dataview
inline fields. `node scripts/obsidian-corpus.mjs` checks the copies;
`--fetch` downloads them again. The test `obsidianCorpus.test.ts` runs
Lumen's own open → save path over every file:

- **Open and save, no edit:** every note and every `.base` comes back
  byte-identical — also when the note was saved by Windows (a byte-order
  mark and CRLF line endings stay; before W4.30 the first edit turned every
  line ending into LF and opening dropped the mark).
- **Properties:** writing a value that is already there changes nothing,
  for every editable property. A key written twice (`tags:` twice is common)
  is shown but not editable: a write could reach only one of the two.
- **Bases:** all 89 views run over their own vault without an error. The
  syntax of the first Bases releases is read too: `sort: - column: x`,
  top-level `display:`, `not()` and `empty()`, and an empty formula.
- **Rename and rename back:** the linking notes come back byte-identical; a
  `./` prefix, a `.md` in a wiki link and a Hebrew file name in a Markdown
  link are kept as written. The one exception is a link written in another
  case (`[[evergreen]]` comes back as `[[Evergreen]]`), which Obsidian
  rewrites the same way.

The WYSIWYG editor writes the note's body again on the first edit (its
Markdown writer has its own spelling of lists and emphasis); edit notes from
another app in the source editor.

pages.title: Side panels
pages.description: The file tree, outline, backlinks, tags, comments, trash and version history — what each side panel shows and how to use it.
pages.md:
Each panel has a **?** button that opens this help at its own section.

## File tree

The left sidebar lists the notes and folders of your vault. Click a note
to open it. Each note and folder has rename and delete, and folders can
take a new note or subfolder. Select several notes to move or delete them
together; a deleted note goes to the trash, and **Undo** brings it back. In
a large vault the folders start collapsed. The sidebar's edge resizes it:
drag it, or focus it and use ← and →.

## Outline

The headings of the open note, as a tree. Click one to jump there. The
outline follows the note as you type.

## Backlinks

Every note that links to the open one with a `[[wiki-link]]`, with the
line around each link. Click a backlink to open that note.

## Tags

Every tag in the vault, from `tags:` in the frontmatter and from `#tags`
in the text, with how many notes use it. Click a tag to filter the file
tree by it.

## Comments

Comments on the shared note, when you collaborate. Each card shows the
author, the text it is anchored to and the replies. Click a card to select
that text; resolve, reply to or delete a comment from its card. Show all
comments or only the unresolved ones.

## Trash

What you deleted in the last 30 days. **Restore** puts a note back where
it was; **Delete forever** removes it now. After 30 days notes are removed
for good.

## Version history

Every kept version of the open note, newest first. A version is kept every
couple of minutes while you type, on every save and when you close the
tab. Pick a version to preview it, with how much it differs from the
current text, and **Restore this version** if you want it back.

pages.title: Ask a PDF
pages.description: Questions about a PDF answered on this device from its own pages — every answer with quotes you can open at their page and line.
pages.md:
In the [PDF reader](/workspace/pdf-reader/), **Ask** opens a question box
beside the pages. The answer comes from the PDF's own text, on this
device, and every claim carries a quote with its **page and line**; a click
on a quote opens that page and marks the words.

## How an answer is made

1. **Text.** pdf.js reads the text of each page. A page without a text
   layer — a scan — is rendered and read by the on-device OCR (Tesseract,
   Hebrew and English).
2. **Passages.** The pages are cut into passages of whole lines (about 150
   words), each knowing its page and lines. They are ranked for the
   question with BM25 (Hebrew-aware: no niqqud, one-letter prefixes such as
   ו־ה־ב־ל peeled) and, when an Ollama on this machine has an embedding
   model, with embeddings too, the two rankings fused. The index is kept
   while the PDF is unchanged.
3. **Answer.** The six best passages go, numbered, to the `pdf-answerer`
   agent — through the agent runtime, so on a local model (Ollama, or the
   in-browser model) under the *local only* policy. It answers in the
   language of the question and quotes the passages word for word.
4. **Check.** A quote counts only when it is in the passage it names (or
   covers at least 85 % of it, the rule the research citations use); it is
   then placed on its page and line. An answer without one checked quote is
   sent back to the model once with the reason; quotes that still don't
   check out are left out, and the panel says how many.

If the passages don't hold the answer, the panel says *"This PDF doesn't
seem to answer that."* instead of guessing.

## Measuring it

`npm run eval:pdf-chat` asks the questions of the PDF golden set (plan
7.10, `eval/golden/pdf-qa`) against your Ollama and reports the share of
answers whose checked quote is on the page that holds the answer (target:
≥ 85 %). `LUMEN_EVAL_MODEL` picks the model; `LUMEN_EVAL_PDF_DIRS` adds the
held-out test split built with the golden seed. The normal test run checks
the retrieval on the same PDFs without a model.

pages.title: PDF reader and highlights
pages.description: Read PDFs in the vault, highlight text (Hebrew included), and keep every highlight as a W3C Web Annotation in a Markdown note that links back to the page.
pages.md:
Lumen opens a PDF from your vault in a reader of its own. You can select
text on a page and highlight it, add a note to a highlight, and search the
whole document. Every highlight is saved in an ordinary Markdown note next
to the PDF, with a link that opens the PDF at that page and flashes the
highlight.

Everything happens on your device. The PDF is never uploaded.

## Open a PDF

- **Command palette** (⌘K / Ctrl+K) → **Open a PDF for reading…** copies a
  PDF from your computer into the vault and opens it.
- **File tree**: click a `.pdf` file in the vault.
- **A link** in any note: `[[paper.pdf]]`, or `[[paper.pdf#page=3]]` to
  open it at page 3.

Pages are rendered only when they come near the screen, so long documents
open quickly. Use **−** / **+** / **Fit width** to zoom, and type a number
in the page box to jump to a page.

## Highlight text

1. Select text on a page.
2. Press **Highlight**, or the **H** key.

The highlight appears over the words and in the **Highlights** list on the
side. Write in the box under a highlight to add a note; it is saved when
you leave the box. **Delete** removes the highlight.

Highlights work the same in right-to-left text: select Hebrew words and the
highlight covers exactly those words on the line.

## The highlights note

The highlights of `paper.pdf` are kept in `paper.pdf.md`, in the same
folder. **Open the notes** in the reader opens it. It holds a readable list:

```markdown
- [[paper.pdf#page=3&highlight=1a2b3c4d|p. 3]] “the sentence you highlighted” — your note
```

Click a link in the preview and the reader opens at that page and flashes
the highlight.

Below the list there is a fenced `json lumen-pdf-annotations` block with
the highlights as [W3C Web Annotations](https://www.w3.org/TR/annotation-model/):
a `FragmentSelector` for the page (`page=3`, in the
[RFC 3778](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3778) form PDF links use),
refined by a `TextQuoteSelector` (the exact text, with a little of the text
before and after it) and a `TextPositionSelector`. Other annotation tools
can read them.

Lumen only rewrites the part of the note between the
`lumen:pdf-annotations` markers. Anything you write above or below them is
kept.

### When the PDF's text changes

A highlight is found again by its quote, not by its position. If the text
on the page moved, was split into lines differently, or a few characters
changed (a re-saved file, a newer PDF engine), the highlight still lands on
the right words. If the text is gone, the highlight stays in the list with
a note that its text wasn't found.

## Search

Type in **Search in this PDF** and press Enter; Enter again goes to the
next match, Shift+Enter to the previous one. Search ignores case, extra
spaces and Hebrew vowel marks (niqqud). ⌘F / Ctrl+F jumps to the search box
while the reader is open, and Esc closes the reader.

## Scanned pages

A page that is only an image has no text to select. The reader says so and
offers **Recognise text (OCR)**: the page's text is recognised on your
device (Hebrew and English, the same OCR as image import) and shown under
the page, where you can search it and highlight it. The recognised text is
not saved with the PDF, so run OCR again to see those highlights after
reopening.

## Limits

- Highlights are made within one page; a selection that runs onto the next
  page is cut at the end of the first.
- Encrypted (password-protected) PDFs don't open.
- The PDF must be in the vault, which needs a browser with the Origin
  Private File System.

A link in any note: [[paper.pdf]], or [[paper.pdf#page=3]] to open it at page 3. Pages are rendered only when they come near the screen, so long documents open quickly. Use − / + / Fit width to zoom, and type a number in the page box to jump to a page.

sections.heading: Highlight text
sections.text: 1. Select text on a page. 2. Press Highlight , or the H key. The highlight appears over the words and in the Highlights list on the side. Write in the box under a highlight to add a note; it is saved when you leave the box. Delete removes the highlight. Highlights work the same in right-to-left text: select Hebrew words and the highlight covers exactly those words on the line.

sections.heading: The highlights note
sections.text: The highlights of paper.pdf are kept in paper.pdf.md, in the same folder. Open the notes in the reader opens it. It holds a readable list: Click a link in the preview and the reader opens at that page and flashes the highlight. Below the list there is a fenced json lumen-pdf-annotations block with the highlights as W3C Web Annotations: a FragmentSelector for the page (page=3, in the RFC 3778 form PDF links use), refined by a TextQuoteSelector (the exact text, with a little of the text before and after it) and a TextPositionSelector. Other annotation tools can read them. Lumen only rewrites the part of the note between the lumen:pdf-annotations markers. Anything you write above or below them is kept.

sections.heading: When the PDF's text changes
sections.text: A highlight is found again by its quote, not by its position. If the text on the page moved, was split into lines differently, or a few characters changed (a re-saved file, a newer PDF engine), the highlight still lands on the right words. If the text is gone, the highlight stays in the list with a note that its text wasn't found.

sections.heading: Search
sections.text: Type in Search in this PDF and press Enter; Enter again goes to the next match, Shift+Enter to the previous one. Search ignores case, extra spaces and Hebrew vowel marks (niqqud). ⌘F / Ctrl+F jumps to the search box while the reader is open, and Esc closes the reader.

sections.heading: Scanned pages
sections.text: A page that is only an image has no text to select. The reader says so and offers Recognise text (OCR) : the page's text is recognised on your device (Hebrew and English, the same OCR as image import) and shown under the page, where you can search it and highlight it. The recognised text is not saved with the PDF, so run OCR again to see those highlights after reopening.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text: Highlights are made within one page; a selection that runs onto the next page is cut at the end of the first. Encrypted (password-protected) PDFs don't open. The PDF must be in the vault, which needs a browser with the Origin Private File System.

pages.title: Print and PDF
pages.description: Print a note or save it as a PDF the way a word processor would, with page numbers (Hebrew numerals too), a header and footer, a table of contents, clean page breaks and embedded fonts.
pages.md:
**Print / Save as PDF…** (in the File menu and the command palette) opens the system print dialog. Choose "Save
as PDF" to get a file. The layout is built for paper, and for Hebrew first.

## What you get

- **Direction and language from the note.** A Hebrew note prints right to
  left, even from the English interface. Because the language is set
  correctly, the PDF's text can be searched and copied.
- **Header:** the note's title on every page except the first.
- **Footer:** "page / pages", as `1 / 5` or in Hebrew numerals `א / ה`.
- **Clean page breaks.** A heading never sits alone at the bottom of a page.
  Tables, rows, images, code blocks, callouts and display math are never
  split. A long table repeats its header row on every page.
- **Forced breaks:** a paragraph that is just `\newpage` or `\pagebreak`.
- **Embedded fonts.** The app's own OFL fonts (Heebo and Frank Ruhl Libre
  for Hebrew, Inter and Source Serif 4 for Latin) are embedded in the PDF,
  so it looks the same on any computer.
- **Light theme on paper,** whatever theme the screen uses.

## Settings, per note

Put these in the note's frontmatter:

```yaml
---
toc: true              # a table of contents (h1–h3) on the first page, with working links
page-numbers: hebrew   # decimal (default), hebrew or none
header: Quarterly memo # header text; "" for none
footer: Confidential   # text before the page number
page-size: Letter      # A4 (default) or Letter
---
```

## On a phone or tablet

The same command works in mobile browsers and in the installed app. When the
browser blocks the print window, as installed apps and iOS do, Lumen prints
from the current page instead.

## Limits

- **Footnotes print at the end of the note,** not at the bottom of each
  page. Chromium's print engine has no per-page footnotes.
- **The table of contents has no page numbers.** Its entries are links,
  which still work in the PDF.
- **Copying from the PDF:** Hebrew and English words copy in reading order.
  A number with a punctuation mark right next to it inside Hebrew text
  (`1:`) can come out of some PDF readers swapped (`:1`). This happens in the
  PDF's text layer, not in what is printed.

## Tested

Ten golden notes are printed on every test run: a Hebrew report, a long
table, a table of contents, footnotes, callouts, code and math, images,
page breaks, an English Letter memo and nested lists. Each is compared with
an approved image (under 1% of pixels may differ). Each PDF's text is also
read back with `pdftotext` to check the reading order, the page numbers and
the embedded fonts.

pages.title: Note properties
pages.description: The note's front matter as typed fields — text, number, date, list, checkbox and link — where an edit changes only that value.
pages.md:
**⌘K → Properties: edit this note's frontmatter** opens a side panel with the
YAML front matter of the open note, one row per key.

## Field types

Each key gets a field that fits its value: **text**, **number**, **date**,
**list**, **checkbox** or **link** (`[[Note]]`). Pick a different type from the
row's menu. A link opens its note, and says so when no note has that name yet.
Values that other notes already use for the same key are offered as you type.

## Adding and removing

At the bottom, type a property name, pick its type and press **Add property**.
A name that already exists is refused, with its name. The **×** on a row
removes that key.

## What changes in the file

Only the value you edited. Comments, the order of keys, quoting and line
endings stay as they were, so the note's history shows one small change. A
value the panel can't show as a field (a nested map, for example) is
read-only here: edit it in the editor.

When the front matter isn't valid YAML, the panel doesn't guess. It says so,
and you fix it in the editor.

pages.title: Quick capture (inbox)
pages.description: Add a thought, task or link to inbox.md in two steps, from the keyboard, the home screen or the share sheet.
pages.md:
Quick capture adds one entry to the end of `inbox.md`, at the root of
your workspace. It takes two steps: open the capture box, type and press
Enter. You stay in the note you were working on. (Sharing is the
exception: it opens the inbox afterwards.)

Each entry is a list item that links to that day's
[daily note](#how-an-entry-looks) and records the time:

```markdown
# Inbox

- [[journal/2026-10-20]] 09:05 call the plumber
- [[journal/2026-10-20]] 14:30 Shared page <https://example.com/a>
  the text that was shared with it
```

If `inbox.md` doesn't exist, the first capture creates it with an
`# Inbox` heading. Quick capture only ever adds text after the last
character of the file. It never changes or reorders what is already
there. If the inbox is open in a tab with unsaved edits, the entry is
added to that open text, so your edits are kept.

Hebrew and other right-to-left text is saved exactly as you typed it,
including bidi marks. The capture box sets its direction from the first
letter you type.

## Opening the capture box

| Where | How |
|---|---|
| Any browser, the installed app, the desktop app | `⌥⌘N` (Windows / Linux: `Ctrl+Alt+N`) or **Quick capture** in the command palette (`⌘K`) |
| Installed app (PWA), home screen / dock / taskbar | Long-press or right-click the Lumen icon, then **Quick Capture**. This opens `/?capture=1`. |
| Desktop app (Tauri) | **File ▸ Quick capture…**, or `⌥⌘N` in the window |

On Windows and Linux, `Ctrl+Alt+N` is skipped when it is really AltGr+N
(which types a letter such as `ń` on some layouts).

In the box, **Enter** saves, **Shift+Enter** starts a new line and
**Esc** closes. **Open inbox** opens `inbox.md` in a tab.

## Sharing to Lumen (Android)

When Lumen is installed as an app on Android, it appears in the system
share sheet. Anything you share to it is added to the inbox as one entry:
the title and link first, then the shared text on the next line. Lumen
then opens the inbox. If this browser can't provide a workspace (no
OPFS), the shared item opens as a new note instead.

The share target uses `GET /?title=…&text=…&url=…`. Only text and links
can be shared. Sharing files would need a POST share target and a custom
service worker.

Sharing from the native iOS and Android apps (Capacitor) is a separate
feature, planned with the native apps (plan 13.3).

## How an entry looks

- `[[…]]` is the path of that day's daily note (folder and file name,
  without `.md`), built from your daily-note folder and file pattern (**Calendar ▸ Daily note settings**). If that
  note doesn't exist yet, the capture creates it from your daily-note
  template, so the link always opens it. An existing daily note is never
  changed.
- The time is your device's local time, as `HH:MM`.
- Blank lines before and after the text are removed, as are spaces at
  the ends of lines. All other lines are indented by two spaces so they
  stay inside the list item.

## A system-wide shortcut on the desktop

In a browser and the installed PWA, `⌥⌘N` works while Lumen's window has
the focus. A shortcut that works from any app needs Tauri's
global-shortcut plugin, which the desktop app doesn't bundle yet. The
frontend already checks for it at startup
(`src/capture/desktopShortcut.ts`). On macOS it registers `⌥⌘N`
(`Alt+Command+N`) when the plugin is there, and otherwise does nothing.
On Windows and Linux it registers nothing: there `Ctrl+Alt+N` is also
what many keyboard layouts send for AltGr+N, and a system-wide shortcut
can't tell them apart, so typing that letter in any app would open Lumen.
To turn it on in your own build:

1. `src-tauri/Cargo.toml`, under the desktop dependencies:
   `tauri-plugin-global-shortcut = "2"`
2. `src-tauri/src/lib.rs`, in `run()` under `#[cfg(desktop)]`:
   `app.handle().plugin(tauri_plugin_global_shortcut::Builder::new().build())?;`
3. `src-tauri/capabilities/default.json`: add
   `"global-shortcut:allow-register"` and `"global-shortcut:allow-unregister"`.

After that, on a Mac, pressing `⌥⌘N` anywhere brings Lumen to the front with the
capture box open. The window permissions this needs (`show`,
`unminimize`, `set-focus`) are already granted.

pages.title: Related notes while writing
pages.description: The notes closest to the paragraph you are writing, and the notes it mentions without a link — on this device, without slowing typing.
pages.md:
**⌘K → Related notes: show / hide** opens a small panel next to the editor.
While you write it shows:

- **Related** — up to five notes closest to the paragraph at the cursor.
  The paragraph's rarest words are searched with the workspace's BM25
  index (Hebrew prefix letters, full/defective spelling and synonyms
  included). When you built an on-device embedding index (Ollama or the
  in-browser model), its results are blended in. A cloud embedding index
  is never used here, so typing sends nothing anywhere. Click a note to
  open it.
- **Mentioned, not linked** — note names that appear in the paragraph
  without a `[[link]]`. They are underlined (dotted) in the editor. **Link**
  turns that mention into `[[Name]]` (or `[[Name|as you wrote it]]`) as one
  edit that Undo takes back. A Hebrew prefix letter stays outside the
  link. The word you are typing is left alone until you move on.

## It never gets in the way of typing

Nothing runs on a keystroke. The panel updates 100 ms after you stop
typing or move the cursor, and ranking a paragraph against 10,000 notes
takes a few milliseconds, so it is up to date well within 150 ms. Your
text changes only when you press **Link**.

## Turning it off

- For **one note**: add `related: false` to its front matter.
- For **a folder**: ⌘K → *Related notes: on / off for this folder* (for the
  folder of the open note; stored on this device).
- Everywhere: close the panel.

pages.title: Daily review (spaced repetition)
pages.description: Review your highlights and question::answer cards a few minutes a day, scheduled by FSRS, with everything kept in the vault.
pages.md:
**Command palette → Daily review** shows today's cards, 5–10 at a time. Each
one comes back just before you would forget it.

## What becomes a card

- **Highlights** from PDFs, books and clipped pages: the same ones as in
  [All highlights](/workspace/highlights/). The card shows the passage; the
  back shows its note and where it is from.
- **Question::answer lines** in any note, one per line:

  ```md
  What does FSRS stand for? :: Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler
  מה בירת צרפת? :: פריז
  ```

  The question needs a space in it or must end with a question mark, so
  Dataview-style fields such as `status:: done` are not cards. Lines in code
  blocks are skipped.

## Reviewing

Read the card and recall it. Press **space** (or the button) to see the
answer, then rate how it went: **1 Again**, **2 Hard**, **3 Good**, **4
Easy**, by key or by button. The name of the source opens the note or the
highlight. Each review has the cards that are due, most overdue first, then
up to 5 new ones a day.

## Where it is kept

The schedule of every card is in `.lumen/review.json` in your vault, so it
syncs with the vault and moves with it to another device. Editing a card's
text in its note keeps its schedule. A card whose highlight or line was
removed stays in the file, with its history, but is no longer shown.

Scheduling is FSRS-5 with its default parameters, asking for 90% recall at
each review.

pages.title: Search operators and #tags
pages.description: Narrow a search with tag:, path:, "phrases", /regex/ and -exclusions; tags written in the text count like front-matter tags.
pages.md:
The search dialog (`⇧⌘F`) and the agents' `search_workspace` tool read the
same operators. Mix them freely with ordinary words. Every operator must
hold (AND), and the words rank the notes that are left.

| Operator | Finds notes… | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `tag:name` | with this tag, in the front matter or as `#name` in the text. `tag:a` also matches nested `#a/b` | `tag:project` |
| `path:text` | whose path contains *text* (any case) | `path:daily/` |
| `"a phrase"` | that contain the phrase as written (any case; Hebrew ignores niqqud) | `"launch plan"` |
| `/regex/flags` | whose text matches the regular expression; flags `i m s u` | `/^TODO:/m` |
| `-anything` | that do **not** match it: `-tag:archive`, `-path:daily`, `-"draft"`, `-/x/`, `-word` | `tag:project -tag:archive` |

A query made only of operators lists the matching notes, newest first,
with the snippet on the match. A `/regex/` that doesn't compile returns no
notes; it never falls back to returning every note.

## Tags in the text

`#tag` anywhere in a note counts as a tag, like `tags:` in the front matter,
in the Tags panel and for `tag:`.

- Letters of any script count: `#פגישות` is a tag.
- `/` nests tags: `#meeting/standup`.
- These are **not** tags: headings (`# Title`), anything in code
  (`` `#x` `` or a fenced block), numbers such as `#42`, and URL fragments
  (`page#section`).

## How it is tested

`src/__tests__/searchOps.test.ts` runs 30 operator queries on a fixed
12-note vault (English, Hebrew, nested tags, tags in code), each checked
against the exact set of notes it must return. The queries run through the
same index the dialog uses.

pages.title: Workspace search (BM25 + Smart)
pages.description: Fast keyword search by default, semantic embeddings on demand.
pages.md:
`⌘K → Search workspace…` opens the workspace search dialog (the palette
shows `⇧⌘F` next to it, but that key toggles focus mode today). Three tabs:

## Search (BM25)

The default: keyword and filename search across every `.md` / `.txt`
note in your workspace, ranked by BM25. Agents use the same search
(`search_workspace`).

- Hebrew-aware: niqqud, final letters (ם/מ, ן/נ…) and the prefix letters
  ו ה ב כ ל מ ש are folded, so *בבית*, *והבית* and *הַבַּיִת* all find
  *בית*. The exact form you typed still ranks first.
- Full and defective spelling meet: *תכנית* finds *תוכנית*, *צהרים* finds
  *צהריים*, *ראיון* finds *ריאיון* (the exact spelling still ranks first).
- Other forms of a word count too, a little less: *אבודות* finds *אבודה*,
  *מזרחנים* finds *מזורחן* (plural, construct and possessive endings).
- A few common synonyms are searched along (*טלפון* / *סמארטפון*,
  *רכב* / *מכונית*, *פגישה* / *ישיבה*…), and common Hebrew words also
  look for their English equivalent, so *מתכון לעוגת שוקולד* finds an
  English *chocolate cake recipe* note — after the Hebrew notes.
- Question words (*מתי*, *איפה*, *למי*, *what*, *when*…) don't count, so
  you can type a question.
- A match in the note's name counts more than one in its text, and the
  whole query found as a phrase counts extra.
- The index is built on the first search and then updated one note at a
  time as you save; a 10 000-note vault answers in a few tens of
  milliseconds.
- Each hit shows a snippet with the match highlighted; the top 40 are
  listed.
- Operators narrow the search: `tag:`, `path:`, `"phrase"`, `/regex/` and
  `-` to exclude. See [Search operators and #tags](/workspace/search-operators/).

Measured by `src/__tests__/hebrewSearch.test.ts` on the probe set
`eval/probes/hebrew-search.json` (30 morphology queries, 30 full/defective
spelling pairs, 5 Hebrew→English queries) and on the HeQ dev split, which
must not drop.

## Smart (semantic)

Hybrid retrieval that fuses BM25 with cosine similarity over OpenAI
`text-embedding-3-small` vectors via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, k = 60).
Finds notes that are semantically related even when the surface words
don't match — a query for *"deep learning"* surfaces a note titled
*"Neural networks"*.

To enable:

1. Switch to the **Smart** tab.
2. Click **Build index** (one-time, then incremental on subsequent runs).
3. Type your query — results re-rank in real time.

**Cost**: each chunk is embedded once and cached in IndexedDB. A 100-note
workspace embeds in ≈ 8s and ≈ 200 K tokens (≈ $0.004 with
`text-embedding-3-small`). Re-indexing only re-embeds chunks whose hash
changed.

## Cross-language: ask in Hebrew, find English sources

With the built-in embedding model (multilingual-e5-small, MIT, runs on this
device), **Smart** search finds English notes, papers and clippings for a
Hebrew question. Hebrew and English land in the same vector space, and BM25
adds its Hebrew→English word list. Each hit in another language than the
question shows a local translation under the original:

- from the local translation engine, when one is installed;
- otherwise from the browser's own on-device translator (Chrome), and only
  when the language pair is already on the device. A search never starts a
  download.
- With neither, the original is shown and the dialog says so. Nothing is
  sent anywhere.

Two limits:
- The Ollama embedding model `nomic-embed-text` is English-only. With it,
  Hebrew questions reach English notes only through keywords, and the dialog
  says so.
- On a 10,000-note vault, ranking takes about 15 ms. Embedding the question
  comes on top of that.

How it is measured:
- `eval/probes/crosslingual-he-en.json` has 50 Hebrew questions over 50
  English research abstracts, written for this repository. Its numbers are
  development numbers. On it, BM25 alone reaches nDCG@10 0.18.
- `npm run eval:crosslingual` measures BM25, e5 and the fusion with the real
  model.
- The held-out check is Belebele questions in Hebrew (heb_Hebr) over its
  English passages (eng_Latn), built locally: Belebele's FLORES text is not
  committed. Pass that split with `LUMEN_EVAL_XL_FILES`.

## Ask Workspace (RAG Q&A)

Type a question, hit Enter — the dialog runs Smart search to find
relevant notes, then sends the top 8 + your question to the configured
chat model. Answers come back with `[1]` / `[2]` citations linked back
to the source notes.

**Use it for**:
- "Summarise everything I've written about onboarding."
- "Which projects mentioned that Q3 launch deadline?"
- "What did I decide about the auth provider?"

The conversation is kept in-dialog — multi-turn follow-ups remember the
prior context.

pages.title: Slides from notes and the canvas
pages.description: Present a note or a canvas as slides, right to left when it's Hebrew, with speaker notes, a presenter view on a second screen, and PDF export.
pages.md:
## From a note

Open the note and run `⌘K → "▶ Present this note as slides"`. The show
starts from the slide where the cursor is.

- An `#` or `##` heading starts a slide, and a `---` line (or `***`) ends
  one. You can use both in the same note. Lines inside code blocks never
  split.
- **Speaker notes**: everything from a line starting with `Note:`,
  `Notes:` or `הערות:` to the end of the slide, or anything inside
  `<!-- notes … -->`. Notes are never shown on the slide.
- **Direction**: each slide follows its own text, so a Hebrew slide is
  right to left. To fix one direction for the whole deck, add `dir: rtl`
  or `dir: ltr` to the frontmatter.

## From the canvas

**Present** in the canvas bar shows the canvas one frame at a time.

- Every Excalidraw frame is a slide.
- Arrows between frames set the order: an arrow from frame A to frame B
  makes B come after A.
- Frames that no arrow points to start the order, in reading order: top to
  bottom, then right to left on a Hebrew canvas and left to right
  otherwise.
- A text in a frame that starts with `Note:` or `הערות:` is that slide's
  speaker notes and isn't shown.
- Slides are drawn with the same Hebrew fixes as the canvas's
  [SVG export](/workspace/canvas-cards/), and note cards show their notes.

## Presenting

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `→` / `←` | Next / previous, following the deck's direction: on a Hebrew deck `←` goes forward, as in a Hebrew book |
| `Space`, `PageDown`, `↓` | Next |
| `PageUp`, `↑`, `Backspace` | Previous |
| `Home` / `End` | First / last slide |
| `Esc` | End the show |

Every slide is prepared before the show starts, so changing slides takes
under 50 ms.

**Presenter view** opens a second window with the current and next slide,
the speaker notes and a timer; its buttons and arrow keys move the show.
In the desktop app with a second screen connected, the slides go full
screen on the other screen and the presenter view stays on yours. In the
browser it's a pop-up window.

**PDF** prints every slide on its own landscape page; choose "Save as
PDF". The text stays text, in its own direction.

pages.title: Student mode
pages.description: Record a lecture, tap Important at the moments that matter, and get a transcript with a ▶ for every sentence, a summary taken from what was said, and review cards linked to their moments. All on this device.
pages.md:
`⌘K` → **Student mode: record a lecture**:

1. Name the lecture and press **Start recording**.
2. When something matters, press **⭐ Important!** or the space bar. A tap
   marks what was said in the 20 seconds before it and the 5 seconds after
   it, since you hear a point a moment before you tap.
3. Press **Stop and process**. The recording is transcribed on this device
   with the local Whisper model, and the lecture note opens.

## The lecture note

`Lectures/<date> <name>.md`, with the recording in `Lectures/audio/`:

- **Summary:** the marked sentences, then the most central ones, in the
  order they were said. Each sentence is copied word for word from the
  transcript, with a ▶ to its moment.
- **Review cards:** one per marked sentence. Its key word is blanked out
  (`Mitosis splits one cell into two ____ cells. :: identical — ▶ 0:21`).
  The cards use the `question :: answer` lines that **Daily review** picks
  up, and each answer links to its moment in the recording.
- **Transcript:** every sentence with its own ▶ (a link into the recording),
  and the marked ones starred.

## Privacy

The recording, the transcript, the summary and the cards stay in your
vault. Transcription uses local Whisper under every AI policy: a lecture is
never sent to a cloud service. The Whisper model is downloaded once, the
first time it is used, and then comes from the browser's cache.

## Limits

- A 90-minute lecture should be processed in under 20 minutes on a laptop
  with a GPU. That has not been measured yet: transcription speed depends on
  the device and on the Whisper model.
- The summary picks sentences; it does not write new ones. When the local
  summarizer (plan 6.11) is installed, it can choose them instead. Whatever
  it returns must be sentences of the transcript.

pages.title: Tasks across the vault
pages.description: Checklist items with dates and priorities in any note, gathered by queries, a Today panel and reminders. Same syntax as the Obsidian Tasks plugin.
pages.md:
Any checklist item in any note is a task. Lumen reads the format of the
[Tasks plugin for Obsidian](https://publish.obsidian.md/tasks/) (MIT),
so notes written for it work unchanged.

```markdown
- [ ] Pay rent #home ⏫ 📅 2026-11-01
- [ ] Draft the report ⏳ 2026-10-27 🛫 2026-10-25
- [x] Book flights ✅ 2026-10-20
- [ ] Water the plants 🔁 every week 📅 2026-10-26
```

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 📅 | due date |
| ⏳ | scheduled date |
| 🛫 | start date |
| ➕ | created |
| ✅ / ❌ | done / cancelled date |
| 🔺 ⏫ 🔼 🔽 ⏬ | priority: highest … lowest |
| 🔁 | recurrence (kept as text) |
| 🆔 / ⛔ | task id / depends on |

Status characters: `[ ]` todo, `[x]` done, `[/]` in progress, `[-]` cancelled.

## Queries

A `tasks` code block lists matching tasks from the whole vault. Ticking
a box there updates the note it came from: only the checkbox and the `✅`
date change, the rest of the line stays exactly as you wrote it. If the note
changed since the list was shown, nothing is written and the block says so.
A recurring task is marked done; Lumen does not add its next occurrence (the
Obsidian plugin does). Only Markdown notes are read for tasks.

````markdown
```tasks
not done
due before in 7 days
tags include #home
sort by due
group by folder
limit 20
```
````

Supported instructions: `done`, `not done`; `due | scheduled | starts |
done | created | cancelled | happens` with `on`, `before`, `after`, `on or
before`, `on or after`, or `in <date> <date>`; `has/no … date`; `priority is
(above|below|not) <level>`; `description | path | folder | filename | heading |
tag` with `includes`, `does not include`, `regex matches /…/`; `tags include`;
`status.type is …`; `is recurring`; `is blocked`; `(a) OR (b)`, `(a) AND (b)`,
`NOT (a)`; `sort by … [reverse]`; `group by …`; `limit N`; `hide …`.
Dates can be `YYYY-MM-DD`, `today`, `tomorrow`, `yesterday`, `in 3 days`,
`2 weeks ago`, `next week`. An instruction Lumen doesn't understand is
shown as an error, never silently dropped.

## Today and upcoming

Command palette → **Tasks: Today and upcoming**. It shows overdue and today's
tasks, then the next 7 days.

## Reminders

In that panel, turn on **Reminders**. While Lumen is open, every task due or
scheduled today gives one notification per day: the browser's, or the
operating system's in the desktop app. Nothing leaves your device.

## Speed

The tasks are indexed with the rest of the vault in a background worker.
A query over 1,000 tasks takes under 100 ms (checked on every change).

pages.title: Very large vaults
pages.description: How Lumen stays fast with 100,000 notes. The search index holds one copy of the text, is kept between sessions, and is updated one note at a time, and big embedding indexes are stored compactly.
pages.md:
This page picks up where [Large vaults and long notes](/workspace/large-vaults/) leaves off. Heavy users reach 50,000 to 100,000 notes, which is where most note apps
slow down. Lumen is measured against a synthetic vault of 100,000 notes:
190 million characters, two thirds of them Hebrew, all with wiki links.

| Measured (100,000 notes) | Limit | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Search: a word, Hebrew with prefixes, a phrase, or a miss | < 200 ms | 73–148 ms |
| Save → in the index | < 50 ms | 9 ms |
| Memory of the search index | < 1.5 GB | 757 MB (it was 4.3 GB) |
| Memory of the notes on the app's main thread | | 67 MB (it was 364 MB) |
| Building the index from scratch, in the background worker | | 7 s (it was 29 s) |

## What makes it fast

- **One copy of the text.** Each note's search text (lower-cased, and for
  Hebrew folded for niqqud, final letters and prefixes) is stored once, in
  chunks of 256 notes, not two or three times per note. A query is one scan
  per chunk.
- **The text lives only in the index.** The app's main thread keeps a small
  summary of each note: its links, tags, frontmatter and length. The graph and
  the tags view read that summary, and renames happen inside the index.
- **Saving touches one chunk.** Saving a note rebuilds only its chunk's search
  text.
- **The index survives a restart.** After changes, the notes the index holds
  are saved in the browser's database while it is idle. The next time the app
  opens, every note whose modification time hasn't changed comes from there,
  and only the others are read from disk. If the saved index is missing or
  out of date, Lumen just builds it in full.
- **All of this runs off the main thread.** The index lives in a worker, so
  opening the app and typing are never blocked by it. The file tree shows a
  limited number of rows per folder.
- **Compact embeddings.** When the semantic index holds more than 50,000
  passages, their vectors are kept in memory as 8-bit integers. That is a
  quarter of the memory, with scores within 1% of the full-precision ones.
  Vectors are unpacked one note at a time, when a search needs them.

## Measuring it yourself

```sh
npm run perf:vault100k                  # 100,000 notes, fails if a limit is broken
npm run perf:vault100k -- --soak 1440   # 24 hours of random edits, deletes and searches
```

pages.title: Safe saves and the vault check
pages.description: Every save lands whole, even if the app is killed half way; the vault check finds damaged files and repairs them with a backup first.
pages.md:
Your notes are real files. A save that stops half way — the battery dies,
the system kills the app, the computer crashes — must never leave a note
cut in two. Lumen makes sure it doesn't, and **Check vault integrity**
finds what other apps, sync clients or an older crash may have left.

## Every save lands whole

Lumen never writes over a note in place. The new text goes to a hidden
file next to the note first; only when all of it is on the disk does that
file take the note's name. If the app stops anywhere in between, the next
time it opens the folder it finishes the save or puts the previous version
back — so each note is always either the version before the save or the
version after it, complete.

| Where the vault is | How |
|---|---|
| **Desktop app** | Temporary file, `fsync`, rename over the note, then the folder is synced too. |
| **Chrome / Edge folder** | The browser writes a swap file and replaces the note when it is complete. |
| **Phone folder (iOS, Android)** | Temporary file `.lumen-tmp~…`, checked for its full size, then renamed; Android syncs the bytes to disk first. |
| **Browser storage on Safari** | The same temporary-file steps inside the write worker. |

This is tested by killing a process with `kill -9` in the middle of
saving, 1,000 times: `npm run test:crash`. After every kill each note is
whole and is its old or its new version.

## Check vault integrity

**Command palette → Check vault integrity** reads every file in the vault
(your own folders only — not `.git`, `.trash` or earlier backups) and opens
a report note. It looks for twelve kinds of damage:

| Problem | Repaired automatically |
|---|---|
| A file cut off in the middle of a character | Yes — the cut character is dropped |
| Text that is not UTF-8 (for example Hebrew saved as Windows-1255) | Yes — converted to UTF-8 |
| A file saved as UTF-16 | Yes — converted to UTF-8 |
| NUL bytes in a text file | Yes — removed |
| An empty file | No — bring a version back from the note's history |
| A JSON or YAML data file (`.canvas`, `.excalidraw`, `.base`, `.json`, `.yaml`) that does not parse | No |
| Front matter that never closes or is not valid YAML | No |
| Two names in one folder that differ only in upper/lower case | Yes — the second is renamed `name (2)` |
| Two names that differ only in Unicode form (é written two ways) | Yes — renamed the same way |
| A link to a note that is not there | No — use **Vault Doctor: Apply Suggested Link Fixes** |
| A temporary file of an interrupted save (Lumen's, the desktop app's, Chrome's `.crswap`) | Yes — removed |
| A save interrupted half way, with the note missing | Yes — the save is finished, or the old version comes back |

Names that differ only in case live side by side on Linux and in browser
storage, but on macOS, Windows and phones one of them hides the other —
which is how notes get lost when a vault moves or syncs.

When something can be repaired, Lumen asks once and then repairs it.
**Before any file is changed, renamed or removed, it is copied to
`.lumen-repair/<date and time>/`** in the vault, so every repair can be
undone by copying the file back. Notes that are open in a tab are left
alone, and a file that changed since the check is not touched.

The check takes a few seconds even for a large vault: 10,000 notes are
checked in under five seconds.

sections.heading: Safe saves and the vault check
sections.text: Your notes are real files. A save that stops half way — the battery dies, the system kills the app, the computer crashes — must never leave a note cut in two. Lumen makes sure it doesn't, and Check vault integrity finds what other apps, sync clients or an older crash may have left.

sections.heading: Every save lands whole
sections.text: Lumen never writes over a note in place. The new text goes to a hidden file next to the note first; only when all of it is on the disk does that file take the note's name. If the app stops anywhere in between, the next time it opens the folder it finishes the save or puts the previous version back — so each note is always either the version before the save or the version after it, complete. Where the vault is How --- --- Desktop app Temporary file, fsync, rename over the note, then the folder is synced too. Chrome / Edge folder The browser writes a swap file and replaces the note when it is complete. Phone folder (iOS, Android) Temporary file .lumen-tmp …, checked for its full size, then renamed; Android syncs the bytes to disk first. Browser storage on Safari The same temporary-file steps inside the write worker. This is tested by killing a process with kill -9 in the middle of saving, 1,000 times: npm run test:crash. After every kill each note is whole and is its old or its new version.

pages.title: Voice notes into the inbox
pages.description: Record a voice note from the capture box; it is transcribed on this device and added to inbox.md, with the recording attached if you want.
pages.md:
In the quick-capture box (⌥⌘N, or the installed app's **Quick capture**
shortcut) press **Record**, speak, and press **Stop**.

- The recording is transcribed **on this device**: by the live Hebrew
  dictation engine when it is installed (plan 6.1), otherwise by local
  Whisper after you stop. Under the **local only** AI policy nothing is
  sent anywhere — the microphone audio never leaves the browser. (The
  first transcription downloads the speech model once; after that it
  works offline.)
- The transcript lands in the box, so you can fix a word before **Add to
  inbox**. A long note gets its first 80 characters as a bold title.
- **Keep the recording** saves the audio under `attachments/`
  (`voice-YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM-<first words>.webm`) and adds a link with its
  time range, e.g. `[▶ 0:00–1:01](<attachments/…webm#t=0,61>)`.
- If no transcript can be made (no model on this device yet), the note
  is kept as audio with the text "Voice note (not transcribed)", so
  nothing you said is lost.

## One tap from the home screen

The address `/?capture=voice` opens the box **already recording**.

- **Installed app (Android, desktop):** long-press the app icon → **Voice
  note**.
- **iPhone / iPad — Shortcuts:** new shortcut → *Open URLs* →
  `https://lumen-md.vercel.app/?capture=voice` (or your own address).
  Add it to the home screen, or say its name to Siri.
- **Android home screen:** add the **Voice note** shortcut of the
  installed app to the home screen. A Quick Settings tile needs the native
  Android app (planned with the mobile builds).
